name: Accelerate (vDSP and vForce element-wise math)
baseline: Plain Swift for loops and map over [Double] and [Float]
verdict_reason: Apple's 2019 claims of large speedups over scalar loops do not hold for simple arithmetic in optimized builds. A 2025 Swift Forums test on an M4 timed vDSP.add and a plain -Ounchecked loop within 2% of each other, and the generated assembly showed the loop auto-vectorized. The re-test covered only addition; vForce transcendental functions and debug builds were not re-measured.
tier_reason: First-party WWDC claims with no device, array size or build settings stated for the vDSP and vForce examples.
claimed_speedup: vDSP approximately three times faster than a for loop and approximately four times faster than a scalar map for Double-to-UInt16 conversion; vForce square root up to 10 times faster than map. Independent re-test of vDSP.add: 1.93 seconds vs 1.96 seconds for a plain Swift loop (n = 1_000_000, m = 10_000). Times rounded to three significant figures from the raw results.
workload: WWDC: element-wise arithmetic on four arrays, type conversion and square root over unstated array sizes. Forum: element-wise addition of two 1,000,000-element Double arrays repeated 10,000 times after warm-up.
hardware: WWDC: not stated; forum re-test: MacBook Air 15-inch, M4, 2025
platforms: iOS 13+, macOS 10.15+ for the Swift vDSP API; C API on all Apple platforms
one_liner: Apple's vectorized array math; claimed 3-10x over scalar loops, but optimized Swift loops match it on simple element-wise arithmetic.
how_it_is_fast: vDSP and vForce are hand-tuned SIMD routines for each Apple CPU, so the vector code is right even in debug builds and on new chips. Since the Swift optimizer auto-vectorizes simple loops in release builds, the advantage is concentrated in work the compiler cannot vectorize, such as transcendental functions, conversions with rounding, FFTs and convolutions.
use_it_when: Debug builds or code that must stay fast without the optimizer
Transcendental functions over large arrays (exp, log, sin, sqrt in vForce)
FFT, convolution, strided access and type conversion with rounding
skip_it_when: Simple element-wise add or multiply in release builds, where the compiler's auto-vectorized loop runs at the same speed
Very small arrays, where call overhead can make a plain loop faster
caveats: WWDC numbers have no device, array size or build settings
The forum arrays are far larger than the L1 cache, so the test is memory-bound, as a numerics developer in the thread pointed out; L1-sized arrays were not re-tested
Only addition was re-tested; the vForce and conversion speedups were not independently re-measured
tradeoffs: Pointer-based C API; the Swift overlay allocates a new result array unless you pass existing storage
